item.title: Africa Aware: Tigray’s renewed war and risks to the wider Horn of Africa
item.description:
Africa Aware: Tigray’s renewed war and risks to the wider Horn of Africa Audio thilton.drupal 11 November 2026

Guests discuss the renewal of conflict in Tigray, its regionalization, the options for containing the violence and possible pathways to peace.

In late September, fighting resumed in Tigray – almost four years after the Pretoria Agreement brought the 2020-22 war to an end.  Disputes over the agreement’s implementation remain unresolved, while federal forces have now taken control of the regional capital Mekelle and set up a caretaker administration. At the same time, there are fears that instability within Ethiopia could draw in neighbouring states, as relations with Eritrea become increasingly strained.

In this episode, guests Dr Mulugeta Gebrehiwot Berhe, Blen Mamo and Dr Abel Abate Demissie join the Africa Programme’s Ahmed Soliman and Lisa Musumba to discuss the renewal of conflict in Tigray, its regionalization, the options for containing the violence and possible pathways to peace.

About Africa Aware

Africa Aware is a podcast from the Chatham House Africa Programme bringing together leading international experts to provide in-depth analysis and sharp insights on the political, economic and social issues shaping African countries, their international relations and the continent as a whole.

You can also listen to Africa Aware on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

Read the Expert Comment from Ahmed Soliman and Dr Abel Abate Demissie here: War has returned to Tigray. This time it may not stay in Ethiopia

item.title: Chatham House Prize 2026 awarded to the women of Afghanistan
item.description:
Chatham House Prize 2026 awarded to the women of Afghanistan News release eoboko.drupal 10 November 2026

Chatham House recognized the women of Afghanistan for their courage and resilience in the face of systematic gender persecution by the Taliban

The women of Afghanistan were awarded the Chatham House Prize 2026 at a ceremony on Monday 9 November.

Chatham House recognized the women of Afghanistan for their courage and resilience in the face of systematic gender persecution by the Taliban, and for their determination to defend the rights and futures of women and girls.

Speaking on a panel that brought together women from the Afghan diaspora, Zahra Joya, the founder and Editor-in-Chief of Rukhshana Media, said the prize ‘sends a powerful message that the world will not forget about us. They will listen to us. They will see our strength and power’.

In a conversation with BBC Chief International Correspondent Lyse Doucet, who moderated the panel, former Chatham House Academy Associate Shaharzad Akbar said that for girls denied an education in Afghanistan the Chatham House Prize shows them ‘they are being remembered, that they are not forgotten’. That, she said, ‘gives them courage’.

Dr Orzala Nemat, the founder and director of Development Research Group LTD, highlighted the voices of the women humanitarian aid workers with whom she collaborates, who asked that the audience help to ‘continue to raise our voices for girls’ education, continue to raise our voices for our right to work’.

Fawzia Koofi, former Deputy Speaker of the Parliament of Afghanistan and President of the Board of Women for Afghanistan, said the Taliban practised double standards in prohibiting girls from accessing secondary and higher education. ‘They have modernized themselves for their own daughters, not for our girls. Their own daughters go to school, university, probably the best universities in the world, but our daughters are confined,’ she said.

Assessing the international community’s engagement with Afghanistan, specifically the UK’s halt on issuing study visas to nationals from certain countries including Afghanistan, Dr Benafsha Yaqoobi, founder and director of The Rahyab Initiative, said the ‘world has failed us in fulfilling their responsibility towards Afghanistan’.  

The Chatham House Prize is awarded to the person, persons, or organization deemed to have made the most significant contribution to the improvement of international relations.

In her opening remarks, Bronwen Maddox, Director and Chief Executive of Chatham House, said of the women of Afghanistan: ‘They have forced governments to ask what recognition of the Taliban would mean and on whose terms. They remind us that how a state treats women is not a domestic matter. It is a measure of whether that state can be trusted at all.’  

On behalf of the women of Afghanistan the award was accepted by Elaha Safdari, goalkeeper for the Afghanistan’s women’s national football team.  

The Prize was presented to her by Chatham House’s president, The Rt Hon Baroness May of Maidenhead, who praised the women of Afghanistan for continuing to speak out. ‘This award belongs to all of them, to every single one of them. But it is also a reminder, and we have heard this from our panel today, of our collective responsibility. We cannot allow the situation facing Afghan women and girls to fade from the international attention,’ she said.

Elaha, who had to leave Afghanistan for the UK when the Taliban returned to power in 2021, thanked the UK government and the sports organisation Girl Power, for supporting her.

She told the audience: ‘Becoming a refugee was never my dream. Leaving Afghanistan meant leaving behind my home, my friends, my teammates, my family.’  She added that football and the work of Girl Power enabled women to be visible. Elaha highlighted there is much work to be done to advance the rights of women in Afghanistan. ‘There are girls who simply want to go to school, play sport, and decide what their futures will look like,’ she said.  

The evening ended with a film that featured contributions from broadcaster Yalda Hakim, the UN’s Susan Ferguson and activist Onaba Payab. The interviews appeared alongside personal reflections from women living in Afghanistan whose words were read out by Dr Orzala Nemat, to ensure their safety. 

A women’s activist said: ‘The international community must recognize that support for Afghan women cannot be episodic or symbolic – it requires sustained engagement, listening to local voices, and holding leaders accountable, all parties.’ A teacher and education activist said of young girls in Afghanistan facing extreme obstacles to education: ‘I hope audiences remember not only their courage, but also the urgent need to ensure that every girl has the freedom, safety and opportunity to learn’. 

The Chatham House Prize 2026 is supported by Axel Hansing and the International Organization for Migration.

Watch the full video of the ceremony here, including the the panel of Afghan political and human rights activists in conversation with Lyse Doucet, Elaha Safdari’s acceptance speech on behalf of all Afghan women, Baroness May, Bronwen Maddox, and testimony from women inside Afghanistan read out by an expatriate Afghan journalist in order to preserve their safety.

item.title: Europe faces faster cyberattacks than ever. But many of the solutions are long known
item.description:
Europe faces faster cyberattacks than ever. But many of the solutions are long known Expert comment thilton.drupal 10 November 2026

Cyberattacks against Europe are becoming more frequent and more damaging. Yet while AI has lowered the barrier to entry, most attacks still exploit old and familiar weaknesses.

Last month, hackers caused tons of food to be thrown away after hacking into refrigerators in around 700 French supermarkets. Within weeks, similar incidents were reported in Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Ireland and elsewhere. Nobody has claimed responsibility, but France has accused Iran of carrying out the ‘unprecedented attack’ against it.

The freezer attacks come after a spate of cyber incidents across Europe in the last few years that have repeatedly exposed familiar weaknesses. Russia’s war against Ukraine has raised the stakes, putting Europe on the front line of hybrid attacks including through cyber operations. 

Four problems stand out: old systems that are never fixed, new technology built without security in mind, increasingly capable attackers aided by AI, and states using cyberattacks as instruments of power, often through proxies. 

Each requires its own response, and Europe is doing better on some fronts than on others. None is a European problem alone, and none will be solved by Europe alone.

Vulnerable legacy systems 

The first problem lies in the weakness already built into the technology Europe runs on. Much of Europe still relies on legacy systems – technology that has reached the end of its life and no longer receives the security patches it needs. The result is a stock of known vulnerabilities that attackers can exploit.

The freezer attacks show what this looks like in practice. They were not technically complex: most of the hacked temperature controllers in France were reportedly legacy systems that no longer receive updates. Operational technology of this kind, which controls physical equipment, often stays in service for decades, long after anyone is updating it. 

This is not just an issue for companies. The UK’s National Audit Office found in 2025 that government departments used ‘hundreds of ageing legacy IT systems.’ Germany’s federal audit office found in 2025 that parts of the federal government’s networks are so outdated they no longer receive security updates.

Part of the problem is visibility: organizations and governments often lack a clear picture of the technology they own and operate. Even when organizations know where the problems lie, replacing old systems is expensive and disruptive. But leaving them in place is becoming increasingly risky.

Replacing these systems is primarily the responsibility of national governments and companies that operate them. But the EU is also pushing for it. In July, the European Central Bank told Europe’s largest banks to replace or update legacy systems as part of planning for AI-enabled threats. The financial sector, however, is far ahead of most other sectors, and replacement will require money, expertise and political commitment.

In the meantime, basic measures, often referred to as ‘cyber hygiene’, can go a long way. According to ENISA, the EU’s cybersecurity agency, two-thirds of the vulnerabilities attackers exploit already have a patch available. Where equipment no longer receives security updates, organizations need to restrict its exposure or replace it. 

Europe does not lack information or rules: ENISA maintains a European Vulnerability Database, national agencies issue regular alerts, and the NIS2 Directive makes managing these risks a legal obligation. What is missing is implementation: turning warnings into action, particularly in smaller organizations, and enforcing rules that many member states have been slow to adopt. 

Technology built without security

The second problem is that too much technology is still being built without security in mind. This is due to market incentives; manufacturers compete on price, features and speed to market, rather than prioritizing security. The costs of insecurity have mainly fallen on customers and society. 

The EU has sought to change this. From December 2027, under the EU’s Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), connected products that do not meet basic security requirements will no longer be allowed on the EU market. Manufacturers will be responsible for their security throughout their lifecycle. 

However, the CRA has limits. Manufacturers are required to report actively exploited vulnerabilities, including those affecting products already on the market. But reporting a flaw does not fix it. 

And for products that manufacturers no longer support, there may be no fix. Someone else then has to act: the shop, hospital or council operating the equipment must know it is affected and have the skills and resources to patch, isolate or replace it. 

The underlying problem is poor-quality software. AI could help strengthen the security of software by identifying and fixing flaws faster than people can. But that depends on vendors using AI tools (with human oversight) before their products reach the market.

More attackers, moving faster

The use of AI by attackers is compounding these problems. AI is accelerating the process by which attackers are finding and exploiting vulnerabilities in insecure products and ageing systems. It is lowering the skills and resources needed to launch attacks and compressing the time defenders have to respond.

This year, frontier AI labs made a series of striking disclosures about their latest models’ cyber capabilities. These capabilities are real, particularly when it comes to exploiting vulnerabilities including in legacy systems. The labs were right to disclose them. But the disclosures also showcased their products, and the hype and catastrophizing that followed have not always helped clarify where priorities should lie. 

AI is not yet changing the nature of the game so much as its speed and scale. ENISA found that attackers in 2025 relied mainly on off-the-shelf AI tools to sharpen skills they already had. Similarly, the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre found that among the incidents it handled, AI had not enabled ‘a novel class of attack’. 

Related work

Is AI really getting out of control?

Instead, the greater danger is that AI-assisted vulnerability discovery gives attackers more opportunities to strike before system owners can apply patches. In response, defenders must be able to act at the same speed. 

Governments have not yet managed to achieve this. The EU, for example, created the European Cybersecurity Alert System to analyse threat and incident data across member states using AI. However, EU auditors recently found that the system had stalled and was not yet working as intended.

A separate challenge is dependence on external providers. Many of the most capable defensive AI tools are developed in the US. Access can be restricted or withdrawn, as US export controls showed in June 2026. Governments need to establish structured ways of working with these companies on early warning, model testing and making defensive tools available to operators of critical infrastructure.

Cyber as a tool of state power

The fourth problem is that states are increasingly using cyber operations as a routine instrument of power, often through proxies. As argued in this Chatham House paper, the war in Ukraine has exposed an entire ecosystem of proxies. The overlap between these actors blurs responsibility and complicates attribution. 

Europe does not lack the tools to respond to state-backed cyber activity. It has mechanisms for public attribution, criminal investigations, sanctions and diplomatic pressure. But these measures have been slow and applied unevenly, which has reduced their collective impact. 

Related work

Holding state-sponsored hackers and other cyber proxies to account

The priority is therefore to use existing instruments more quickly and consistently. This requires coordinating responses across Europe and with international partners.

An EU-wide response is only as effective as the national systems underpinning it. Yet all but two member states missed the deadline to adopt the NIS2 Directive, which requires critical sectors to manage risks and report serious incidents. Member states need to improve information sharing, strengthen reporting and practise their responses to attacks. 

Internationally, states have already agreed not to attack critical infrastructure or knowingly allow their territory to be used for malicious cyber activity. The UN’s new Global Mechanism on ICT security is where Europe and its partners should push to make those commitments count.

Familiar threats, less time

The attacks of the recent weeks may look new, but they tell a familiar story: known weaknesses, insecure products, more capable attackers and slow, fragmented responses. What has changed is the timescale. 

Europe has already written many of the rules. Its member states now need to secure or replace existing technology, ensure that what comes next is secure by design, put AI to work for defenders, and rehearse a coherent response with partners. 

That means not only strengthening Europe’s ability to withstand and recover from attacks, but also its capacity to disrupt those responsible and impose costs that deter future operations.
